findings.title: Background legacy writes inherit the request context and get cancelled when the request ends.
findings.body: Each goroutine builds its timeout context from the request `ctx`. When the handler returns `created`, the apiserver cancels the request context, so the legacy Create usually fails with `context canceled` almost as soon as it starts. Legacy storage then quietly drifts away from unified storage, which defeats the "safe measure" this mode exists for. The same problem is in the Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) goroutines. Fix: derive the context from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before adding the 10s timeout, e.g. `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), time.Second*10, ...)`.

findings.title: A failed unified-storage Create is recorded as a legacy failure.
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage failures then show up in the legacy metric and never in the storage metric. Use `recordStorageDuration`.

findings.title: Delete records the storage metric with the object name as the kind label.
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. Successful deletes are then filed under a wrong kind label. Each deleted object name also creates a new Prometheus series, so the number of series grows without bound. Use `options.Kind`.

findings.title: A failed unified-storage Update is recorded as a legacy failure.
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the error is recorded through `recordLegacyDuration`. Storage failures are then attributed to the legacy store. Use `recordStorageDuration`.

findings.title: The async legacy DeleteCollection is recorded as a storage operation.
findings.body: The goroutine that runs `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` records its result with `recordStorageDuration`. The storage metric then counts DeleteCollection twice, and legacy failures never appear in the legacy metric. Use `recordLegacyDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy Update now re-applies the raw objInfo instead of the object unified storage stored.
findings.body: The old code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper{updated: obj}`, so legacy received exactly the object unified storage had saved. Now legacy runs `objInfo.UpdatedObject` against its own copy of the old object. Two things can go wrong. Preconditions such as the resourceVersion or UID from unified storage can fail with a conflict on legacy. Patches can also produce a different result there. Either way the async legacy update fails or writes different data. Fix: pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` to `d.Legacy.Update`.

findings.title: Delete puts d.Log into the context instead of the logger that carries name, kind and method.
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the name, kind and method values built on the line above. Every other method stores `log`. Use `log`.
